questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the relationship between privacy and consent?
options: They are interchangeable terms for the same concept
Consent is a broader concept that fully contains privacy
Privacy is the individual's underlying right to control their personal data; consent is just one specific mechanism for lawfully processing data when consent is the legal basis relied on
Privacy only applies to Salesforce data, while consent applies to all other data
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit: privacy is the right, consent is one mechanism among several possible legal bases for respecting that right -- not every lawful use of data requires consent.

questions.q: How does this lesson describe the key difference between GDPR's opt-in model and CCPA's opt-out model?
options: GDPR defaults to 'no' processing until an affirmative basis is established; CCPA defaults to 'yes' collection/sale until the individual actively opts out
Both use the same default, just enforced by different regulators
GDPR only applies to Salesforce orgs hosted in Europe
CCPA requires more paperwork but has the same default as GDPR
questions.explain: The lesson calls these opposite starting assumptions: GDPR's opt-in default requires an affirmative legal basis before processing, while CCPA's opt-out default allows processing/sale unless the individual acts to stop it.

questions.q: What role does this lesson say the Individual object plays in Salesforce's privacy tooling?
options: It stores a company's financial records
It replaces the Contact object entirely in every Salesforce org

It's intended as the place that consolidates a person's privacy-relevant preferences -- such as a do-not-process flag and the purposes/legal basis data is being used under -- across the records representing them
It is only used for tracking employee performance reviews
questions.explain: The lesson describes the Individual object as the consolidation point for a person's consent and restriction status, linked from Lead, Contact, or Person Account records representing that same person.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why are "withdrawing consent" and "restricting processing" treated as genuinely different requests?
options: They are not different -- both always require immediate deletion of all the individual's data
Restricting processing can only be requested by companies, never by individuals
Withdrawing consent only applies to CCPA, and restriction only applies to GDPR

Withdrawing consent revokes a specific permission previously given (processing on that basis generally must stop); restricting processing is a narrower, often temporary pause that doesn't necessarily withdraw consent or delete data
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes a full revocation of a legal basis (consent withdrawal) from a temporary pause on active use (restriction), noting a process with only one blunt option can't represent either correctly.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say consent should be tracked as an ongoing record rather than a one-time action?
options: Because Salesforce automatically deletes consent records after 30 days regardless of policy
Because consent never changes once given, so tracking it is only a formality

Because an organization has to be able to prove its basis for processing someone's data at any later point -- what was asked, when, and whether it was given, withdrawn, or restricted -- not just assume it asked once
Because the Individual object cannot store more than one value per person
questions.explain: The lesson frames consent as data requiring the same governance rigor as any other governed field -- an owner, quality expectations, and the ability to prove the current and historical state of consent.
